title: Born Again into a Living Hope
sum: Peter writes to 'the chosen temporary residents of the Dispersion' across five regions of Asia Minor (1:1-2). He blesses God, who gave them new birth into a hope that is alive through Christ's resurrection, an inheritance kept in heaven, and a salvation ready to be revealed (1:3-5). Their present trials are like fire testing gold: their faith, once proven, will bring praise when Christ is unveiled (1:6-9). The prophets searched for this salvation, and angels long to look into it (1:10-12).

Then the commands begin. Since they were ransomed from an empty inherited way of life by the blood of Christ, the flawless lamb, they are to be holy as God is holy, to live in fear during their stay as resident aliens, and to love one another from a pure heart, because they were born again from God's word, which remains forever (1:13-25).
readings: A letter of hope to the uprooted

Read from the readers' side, the chapter gives people who had lost their place in family and town a new identity: chosen, born again, heirs of an estate no one can seize, and part of a story the prophets foretold. The losses are real; the hope is greater.
Israel's story, retold for the nations

Almost every line uses Israel's words: chosen, Dispersion, sprinkled blood (Exodus 24), inheritance, ransom (Deuteronomy 7:8), the flawless lamb, 'You will be holy' (Leviticus 19:2), Isaiah's word that remains forever. Gentile believers are invited into Israel's exodus and exile.
A baptismal sermon?

Some scholars have read 1:3-4:11 as a sermon given at a baptism, because of the new birth (1:3, 23), the newborn babies (2:2) and the baptism of 3:21. Others reply that the letter only reminds readers of their baptism, as Paul does (Romans 6:3-4).

views.H: The five regions covered most of Asia Minor north of the Taurus Mountains. The readers' 'futile way of life that your fathers passed on to you' (1:18) is the main reason many read them as Gentile converts who had left their families' gods (for the other views, see the note at 1:1). In that world, leaving the ancestral gods was seen as disloyalty to family and city.
views.C: The opening's use of Paul's language (the greeting, 'Blessed be the God and Father', 1:3; compare 2 Corinthians 1:3 and Ephesians 1:3) and its polished Greek are part of the authorship debate: some take them as signs of a Roman circle familiar with Paul's letters, others of a secretary such as Silvanus, others of shared early Christian tradition.
views.L: 1:3-12 is one long blessing built in three steps: hope (1:3-5), joy in trials (1:6-9), the prophets and angels (1:10-12). Each step is hooked to the last by a relative phrase, 'in which' (1:6) and 'about which' (1:10), so the passage runs on almost without a break; the SBL text puts full stops only at 1:5, 1:7 and 1:9. The chapter is framed by 'new birth' (1:3, 23) and by the readers as foreigners (1:1, 17), a theme the letter closes with 'Babylon' (5:13).
views.J: Holiness (Leviticus 11:44-45; 19:2), the ransom from Egypt, the Passover lamb and Isaiah 40's word of comfort to exiles all come from Israel's Scriptures. Peter never says 'Israel' or 'the Jews'. Jewish readers have read the same texts as God's word to Israel, a covenant that the Torah says will last.
views.T: 1:2 names Father, Spirit and Jesus Christ together, and 1:11 speaks of 'the Spirit of Christ' in the prophets; both became texts in the church's teaching on the Trinity. 1:18-19 shaped the language of redemption by Christ's blood in Christian worship.

deep.b:
The address names them only as 'the chosen temporary residents of the Dispersion' (1:1). Who they were has been read three ways.

Jewish believers. 'Dispersion' was the Jews' own word for their scattered communities, and Peter was the apostle to the circumcised (Galatians 2:7-8). Eusebius, following Origen, says Peter 'preached in Pontus, Galatia, Bithynia, Cappadocia, and Asia to the Jews of the dispersion' (Church History 3.1.2). Calvin agreed: the word 'can apply only to the Jews', and Peter 'designed this Epistle more especially for the Jews'.

Mixed churches. Calvin's translator, John Owen, noted that 'nothing decisive' shows the letter was 'written only to believing Jews', while 4:3 'seems clearly to shew that Peter included the believing Gentiles'.

Mostly Gentiles. Many modern interpreters read three clues this way: the readers were ransomed from 'the futile way of life that your fathers passed on to you' (1:18), they once did 'what the Gentiles want' (4:3-4), and they did not know God before (1:14). The NET Bible's notes, for example, take 'Dispersion' as a picture used of Gentile Christians. Those who hold the other views reply that converts in a mixed church could be described the same way.

Whichever is right, Peter speaks to them in Israel's words throughout, and calls the outsiders 'the Gentiles' (2:12). Whether 'temporary residents' and 'resident aliens' (1:1, 17; 2:11) describe a social fact or a spiritual one is the other main question about the readers: see the note at 2:11 and the opening pages (Who it was for).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the letter's frame is an exile's road from Babylon
deep.b: The letter opens with 'the Dispersion' (1:1), quotes, in 1:24-25, the opening of Isaiah's message of comfort to the exiles in Babylon (Isaiah 40:6-8), and closes with greetings from 'Babylon' (5:13). I suggest that the frame is deliberate: the writer, in 'Babylon', writes to scattered people as Jeremiah wrote from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon, telling them to seek the good of the city where they lived (Jeremiah 29:7), which is close to the advice of 2:12-17. This overlaps with the common scholarly view that the letter reads the church's situation through Israel's exile, but goes further in reading Jeremiah 29 as the letter's model. The letter never quotes Jeremiah 29, so this is a suggestion only.

echoes: Exodus 24:7-8; Leviticus 11:44-45; Leviticus 19:2; Deuteronomy 7:8; Exodus 12:5; Isaiah 40:6-8; Isaiah 52:13-53:12; Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 1:3; Ephesians 1:3; John 3:3; John 20:29; Titus 3:5; James 1:2-3; James 1:18

settings.by: Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ (5:12 names Silvanus as the one 'through' whom he wrote)
settings.to: Believers scattered across Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, meeting in house churches in towns and villages: probably mostly Gentile converts, though ancient and Reformation readers took them to be Jewish believers of the Dispersion
settings.when: From 'Babylon' (5:13), probably Rome, in the 60s if Peter wrote it, or later in the century if a Petrine circle wrote it in his name
settings.why: To tell people who had become outsiders in their own towns who they now are: chosen by God, made holy by the Spirit, covenant people sprinkled with Christ's blood. The words 'temporary residents' and 'Dispersion' make their unsettled life part of God's story instead of a mark of shame.
views: The traditional view: the apostle, perhaps with Silvanus' help, wrote to churches in Asia Minor from Rome before his death under Nero.
Many critical scholars hold that followers of Peter in Rome wrote in his name after his death, to bring his authority to the churches of Asia Minor.
Eusebius (Church History 3.1.2) and Calvin read the 'Dispersion' as Jewish believers, Peter being the apostle to the circumcised.
Many modern readers, pointing to 1:18 and 4:3, think the churches were mostly Gentile; Calvin's translator John Owen held that they included believing Gentiles.

settings.what: The opening blessing: a living hope
settings.to: The same churches, hearing the letter read aloud
settings.when: While they were facing 'trials of many kinds' (1:6)
settings.why: To set their suffering inside a larger frame before giving any commands: they were born again, they have an inheritance no one can take, God guards them, and their trials are a test that will end in praise. Knowing that the readers were slandered and pushed to the margins explains why the letter begins with what they have, not with what they must do.

settings.what: Be holy: the call and its grounds
settings.why: To turn new identity into a new way of life. The readers, ransomed from their ancestral way of life, are to be holy, live in fear of God, and love one another as family, because they are now God's house and priesthood (2:5, 9). For Gentiles who had lost their families' approval, the call to be 'holy' gave a reason for their difference and a new family to belong to.

title: Living Stones, Resident Aliens
sum: Like newborn babies, the readers are to crave the milk of the word (2:1-3). Coming to Christ, the living stone that people threw out but God chose, they are being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood (2:4-5). A chain of stone texts from Isaiah and the Psalms shows Christ as honor for believers and a stumbling stone for others (2:6-8), and Israel's titles from Sinai and the prophets are given to them: a chosen family, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own people (2:9-10).

As resident aliens among the Gentiles, they are to live so well that slanderers will glorify God (2:11-12). They are to submit to the emperor and governors and honor all people (2:13-17). Household slaves are to submit even to crooked masters, because Christ suffered unjustly and left them a model to trace; Isaiah 53 describes his suffering, by whose welts they were healed (2:18-25).
readings: The church as temple and priesthood

Read with 2:4-10 at the center, the chapter is about what kind of community the readers are: a house where God lives, a priesthood that offers the sacrifices of whole lives, a people who tell out God's acts. This reading has fed both the Reformation's priesthood of all believers and Catholic and Orthodox teaching on the common priesthood of the baptized.
A strategy for life under pressure

Read with 2:11-25 at the center, the chapter is practical advice to a small, slandered group: do good, submit where you can, give no one a real reason to accuse you, and hope that outsiders will be won. Scholars differ on whether this is wise engagement with society or accommodation to its hierarchies.
Hard words for slaves

Read from the slaves' side, the passage asks the most of the least powerful. Some readers find its comfort real: Christ stands with the unjustly beaten slave, and God calls the master's harshness unjust. Others note how this teaching was later used to defend slavery, and read it as a first-century strategy, not a law for all time.

views.H: The provinces had cities with temples to the emperor, and governors who judged disputes. Household slaves were a large part of urban populations. Peter's advice fits a small minority with little legal protection, whose neighbors already called them wrongdoers (2:12).
views.C: The stone texts (Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 8:14) appear together in Romans 9:33 and in the Gospels and Acts, which suggests a collection used in early Christian teaching. 2:21-25 is often thought to use an early hymn or confession built on Isaiah 53. The household code (2:13-3:7) is compared with Ephesians 5-6, Colossians 3-4 and Greek works on household management, and its purpose is debated. John H. Elliott read the letter as giving a home and identity to people in conflict with their society; David Balch read the code against Greek philosophy on household management and wrote on 'acculturation' in 1 Peter; Elliott himself called their conclusions 'diametrically opposed', as Moses Chin reports.
views.L: The chapter turns on two images: building (stone, house, cornerstone) and status (chosen, priests, people, then resident aliens, slaves). The word 'trickery' (dolos) links 2:1, the milk 'with no trickery' (2:2) and Christ in whose mouth no trickery was found (2:22).
views.J: 2:9-10 gathers Exodus 19:6, Isaiah 43:20-21 and Hosea 1-2, texts about Israel, and applies them to a church that was probably mostly Gentile. Whether this means the church has taken Israel's place, has been joined to Israel, or simply borrows Israel's language is a central question; see the topic church-israel. Jewish interpreters read Isaiah 53 of Israel or a righteous figure in Israel.
views.T: 2:5 and 2:9 are the classic texts for the common priesthood of the faithful (Catholic and Orthodox) and the priesthood of all believers (Protestant): see the card below. 2:13-17 is a key text in Christian teaching on government, alongside Romans 13.

deep.b:
Peter strings together three texts about a stone: Isaiah 28:16 (the cornerstone God sets in Zion), Psalm 118:22 (the stone the builders threw out) and Isaiah 8:14 (the stone that makes people stumble). Jesus applied Psalm 118:22 to himself (Matthew 21:42), Peter quoted it to the council (Acts 4:11), and Paul joined Isaiah 28:16 and 8:14 in Romans 9:33. The same stone means honor to those who believe and stumbling to those who refuse.

Peter adds something none of the other passages say: the believers are stones too, 'stones that live', built on the living stone into a house for God (2:5). Ephesians 2:20-22 has a similar picture, with Christ Jesus 'as the cornerstone' and the believers 'being built together, to be a home for God in the Spirit'.

deep.h: The household code and the emperor
deep.b:
2:13-3:7 is one of the New Testament's 'household codes' (compare Ephesians 5:21-6:9; Colossians 3:18-4:1; Titus 2:1-10). Peter's version is unusual. It begins with the emperor and governors, speaks to slaves but not to masters, and to wives at length, many of them with unbelieving husbands. It speaks to the weaker party in each pair as a moral agent who chooses how to act before God.

Peter tells the readers to 'give honor to the king' but to fear God (2:17). The emperor is honored as all people are honored, not worshiped. On whether Christians must always obey the state, see the card at Romans 13; on slavery, the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon; on wives, the card at Ephesians 5.

deep.title: Claude's theory: 'trickery' as the thread of 2:1-22
deep.b: The word dolos, 'trickery', appears in 2:1 (take it off), in 2:2 as the milk with no trickery (adolos), in 2:22 (no trickery in Christ's mouth, from Isaiah 53:9) and again in 3:10 (lips that do not speak trickery, from Psalm 34). I suggest that Peter chose the Isaiah and Psalm texts partly because they share this word, so that the whole section moves from removing trickery, to feeding on what has none, to imitating the one who had none. Commentators note the 2:1-2 wordplay; the link to 2:22 and 3:10 is my own reading.

echoes: Psalm 34:8; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16; Isaiah 8:14; Exodus 19:5-6; Isaiah 43:20-21; Hosea 1:6-10; Hosea 2:23; Isaiah 53:4-12; Romans 9:25-33; Romans 13:1-7; Ephesians 2:19-22; Ephesians 6:5-9; Matthew 21:42; Acts 4:11; Matthew 5:16

settings.to: The churches, as people slandered by their neighbors
settings.when: The same letter, at the turn to its practical teaching
settings.why: To give a small, accused minority a way to answer slander: live so well that the charges cannot stick, and hope the accusers will come to glorify God. The words assume that the readers' neighbors were watching them closely.

settings.to: All the believers in the five provinces, under Roman governors
settings.when: Under the emperor and his provincial governors. Around AD 112 Pliny, governor of Bithynia-Pontus, made people accused as Christians offer incense and wine to the emperor's image
settings.why: To show that Christians were not rebels: they honor the emperor and do good, and the governors' task is to commend those who do good. For people suspected of disloyalty, this was protection and witness at once. The verse 'Fear God. Give honor to the king' also set a limit: worship belonged to God alone.
views: Many churches read the passage, with Romans 13, as a lasting teaching that Christians should obey the state except where it commands sin.
Others read it as advice for a powerless minority in Rome's empire, to be weighed against texts that resist unjust rulers (Acts 5:29; Revelation 13).

settings.to: Christian household slaves, many with unbelieving masters, hearing the letter read in the assembly
settings.why: To give slaves, who could be beaten for their faith or for nothing, a way to bear unjust suffering without returning evil, and to tell them that God sees it and that Christ himself suffered the same way. The passage addresses slaves as full members and moral agents. It binds Christian slaves in Roman households; whether it says anything about slavery as an institution is debated (on the churches' teaching now, see the cards at Ephesians 6 and Philemon).
views: Christ is shown standing with the beaten slave, and God calls the master's harshness unjust.
The passage accepted slavery as it was and was later used by slaveholders to demand obedience; its comfort cannot be separated from that history.

settings.what: Christ the suffering servant (perhaps an early hymn)
settings.by: Peter, perhaps using a hymn or confession
settings.to: The slaves first, then the whole church
settings.why: To give the slaves, and all who suffer unjustly, the pattern of Christ as Isaiah 53 describes him: sinless, silent under abuse, bearing others' sins, healing by his wounds.
views: Many scholars think the passage, with its rhythm and its relative clauses ('who ...'), uses an existing hymn or confession.
Others see Peter shaping Isaiah 53 himself to fit the slaves' situation, as the shift to 'you were healed' shows.

traditions.q: All believers are 'a holy priesthood' that brings 'spiritual sacrifices' and 'a royal priesthood' (2:5, 9). What is this common priesthood, and how does it relate to ordained ministers? (Whether the church still has an ordained priesthood, now that Christ is the one high priest, is the card at Hebrews 7:23-28; whether the church has priests as Israel had Aaron's sons is the card at Exodus 28.)
views: 'The whole community of believers is, as such, priestly' (Catechism 1546, citing 1 Peter 2:5, 9). The baptized exercise this priesthood 'through their participation, each according to his own vocation, in Christ's mission as priest, prophet, and king'. The ministerial priesthood of bishops and priests and the common priesthood both share, 'each in its own proper way, in the one priesthood of Christ', but 'they differ essentially'; the ministerial priesthood serves the common one (Catechism 1547, citing Vatican II, Lumen Gentium 10).

Philaret's Longer Catechism counts Orders among the seven sacraments: in it 'the Holy Ghost, by the laying on of the Bishop's hands, ordains them that be rightly chosen to minister sacraments, and to feed the flock of Christ', in three degrees, bishop, priest and deacon (questions 357-360). A joint Orthodox-Catholic theological consultation in North America (2019), a dialogue text with 'no authority beyond that of the dialogue commission itself', says the titles of 2:9 'apply to all the baptized, before there are further distinctions within the community', that the Eucharist 'is, properly speaking, the priestly act of the entire People of God', and that the bishop or priest who presides 'represents Christ as the head of the Church'.

The Lutheran confessions cite 2:9 for the church's right to call its own ministers: 'Ye are a royal priesthood. These words pertain to the true Church, which certainly has the right to elect and ordain ministers since it alone has the priesthood' (Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope 69, in the Book of Concord). Luther had written in 1520: 'Through baptism all of us are consecrated to the priesthood, as St. Peter says in I Peter 2:9', with no difference among Christians 'but that of office' (To the Christian Nobility).

The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 32), citing 2:5 and 2:9, says every believer shares in Christ's anointing, 'to present myself to him as a living sacrifice of thanks' and 'to strive with a free conscience against sin and the devil'. Calvin on 2:9: believers are 'royal priests, and, indeed, in a more excellent way, because ye are, each of you, consecrated in Christ, that ye may be the associates of his kingdom, and partakers of his priesthood'.

The Episcopal Church's catechism: 'The ministers of the Church are lay persons, bishops, priests, and deacons.' Lay people are 'to represent Christ and his Church; to bear witness to him wherever they may be'; a priest is to represent Christ 'particularly as pastor to the people', to administer the sacraments, and 'to bless and declare pardon in the name of God' (Book of Common Prayer 1979, 'An Outline of the Faith').

The Baptist Faith and Message cites 2:4-10, with Exodus 19:5-6, in its article on evangelism: 'It is the duty of every child of God to seek constantly to win the lost to Christ by verbal witness'. A church's 'two scriptural offices are that of pastor/elder/overseer and deacon', and 'each member is responsible and accountable to Christ as Lord' (2000, articles 6 and 11).

title: The Spirits in Prison
sum: Wives with unbelieving husbands are to submit and win them over without a word, by a gentle and calm life, like Sarah; husbands are to live with their wives with knowledge and honor them as co-heirs of the grace of life (3:1-7). Then to all: be of one mind, return blessing for abuse, and live by Psalm 34 (3:8-12). If they suffer for doing right they are blessed; they are not to fear, but to count Christ holy as Lord and be ready to give a gentle defense of their hope (3:13-17).

The reason is Christ, who suffered once for sins to bring them to God, was put to death in the flesh and made alive in the spirit. In the spirit he went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison, who disobeyed in Noah's day, when eight were carried safe through water. That water has its counterpart in baptism, which now saves, as the pledge of a good conscience to God, through the resurrection of Christ, who is at God's right hand with all powers under him (3:18-22).
readings: Christ's victory over the powers

Read with 1 Enoch and 2 Peter 2:4-5, the 'spirits in prison' are the angels who sinned before the flood. The risen Christ, on his way to God's right hand, proclaims his victory over them (3:22). The readers, a small minority like Noah's eight, can face hostile powers without fear.
Christ among the dead

Read with 4:6 and the creeds, the passage tells of Christ's descent to the dead between Good Friday and Easter, to proclaim salvation to those who had died before him. This is the reading of the Catholic Catechism, of the Orthodox Longer Catechism and of the Easter icon of the Anastasis.
Christ preaching in Noah

Augustine read it as the pre-existent Christ, 'in the spirit', preaching through Noah to the people of his day, whose spirits are now imprisoned. This keeps the passage within the Bible's own story of Noah, 'a herald of righteousness' (2 Peter 2:5).

views.H: A Christian wife in a Roman home was expected to share her husband's gods; Plutarch said so in his Advice to Bride and Groom. The 'defense' of 3:15 could be an answer to a neighbor's question or before a magistrate. The flood story was known well beyond Judaism, and the story of the Watchers in 1 Enoch was known to New Testament writers (Jude 1:14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9).
views.C: Many scholars think 3:18-22 uses an early creed or hymn (Christ died, was made alive, went, is at God's right hand). Many today read the 'spirits in prison' as the fallen angels of 1 Enoch, a reading argued by Friedrich Spitta; Stanley Porter credits Edward Selwyn (1946) with its wide influence. The household code's purpose is debated (see chapter 2).
views.L: The chapter moves from silent witness (3:1, 'without a word') to spoken defense (3:15), and from the readers' suffering for doing good (3:17) to Christ's suffering for sins (3:18). The flood and baptism are joined by water and by the number of the saved.
views.J: The wife's model is Sarah (Genesis 18:12). Psalm 34 is quoted at length. The flood story, the Watchers of Genesis 6:1-4 and their prison are developed in 1 Enoch, which the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts as Scripture and Jude quotes. Isaiah 8:12-13 is applied to Christ.
views.T: 3:18-20 is the main text for the descent into Hades (the creeds' 'he descended into hell'), and 3:21 for baptism as saving: both are on cards below. 3:15 is the charter of Christian apologetics.

deep.h: Wives and husbands: what the first readers heard
deep.b:
Peter speaks first to wives who had become Christians while their husbands had not (3:1). In a Roman household the husband chose the family's gods. Plutarch's Advice to Bride and Groom (section 19) told a wife 'to worship and to know only the gods that her husband believes in' and to 'shut the front door tight upon all queer rituals and outlandish superstitions'. A Christian wife had already broken that rule. Peter does not tell her to leave or to give up her faith. He tells her to stay, to live so that her husband might be won 'without a word', and not to be 'frightened by any terror' (3:6).

To husbands he gives one verse (3:7), probably because fewer of them had unbelieving wives, or because there were fewer Christian husbands. They are to live with their wives 'with knowledge', honor them, and remember that the wife is a co-heir of the same grace. A husband who did not would find his prayers cut off.

On how far the call to 'submit' binds Christian marriages today, this site's card at Ephesians 5 sets out the churches' views side by side; Peter's passage raises the same question and does not repeat it here.

deep.h: The spirits in prison: the full picture
deep.b:
Who were the spirits? (1) The angels who sinned in Noah's time (Genesis 6:1-4). 1 Enoch tells of these 'Watchers' bound under the earth until judgment: 'This place is the prison of the angels. They will be held here forever' (1 Enoch 21:10). Jude 1:6 and 2 Peter 2:4-5 also speak of angels kept in chains and, in 2 Peter, link them to Noah. In the New Testament 'spirits' usually means non-human spirits. (2) The human dead of Noah's generation, or all the dead before Christ. (3) The living people of Noah's day, now dead, to whom Christ preached through Noah.

When did he go? Between his death and resurrection (the traditional Catholic and Orthodox reading); after his resurrection, on his way to heaven (many who hold the angel reading, since 'went' in 3:19 matches 'traveled into heaven' in 3:22); or in Noah's day (Augustine, followed by Thomas Aquinas, who judged it 'a better exposition' than the descent reading).

What did he proclaim? Ekeryxen means to announce as a herald, not necessarily to offer salvation. It may be victory and judgment over the angels (compare 3:22), good news to the righteous dead (the Catholic Catechism: 'to free the just who had gone before him'), or a call to repentance in Noah's day. Calvin read the spirits as 'souls separated from their bodies', the godly dead, waiting in a 'watchtower' of hope. The Latter-day Saints read 3:19 with 4:6 as Christ organizing the preaching of the gospel to the dead (Doctrine and Covenants 138).

Augustine admitted he found the passage very hard (Letter 164), and the church has never settled one reading of it.

The creed's clause. The Apostles' Creed says Christ 'descended into hell' (Latin descendit ad inferos, 'he went down to those below'); the Nicene Creed has no such clause. The Apostles' Creed in its present wording most likely took shape in southern Gaul around the middle of the 400s. Churches have explained the clause with 3:19 (the Catholic Catechism, Philaret's Longer Catechism), without it (the Heidelberg Catechism, as Christ's anguish; the Westminster Larger Catechism, as his remaining under the power of death until the third day), or as a mystery not to be probed (the Lutheran Formula of Concord).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the herald and the herald
deep.b: 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah 'a herald of righteousness' (keryx), and 1 Peter 3:19 says Christ 'made a proclamation' (ekeryxen, the same root) to the spirits disobedient in Noah's day. I suggest that the two letters draw on a shared tradition in which Noah's preaching and Christ's proclamation were set side by side, the second the counterpart of the first, as baptism is the counterpart of the flood (3:21). This would explain why 1 Peter singles out Noah's generation at all. It overlaps with the Augustinian reading, which joins Christ and Noah, but does not require that Christ preached through Noah; it only claims that the herald image linked them for the first readers.

echoes: Genesis 18:12; Psalm 34:12-16; Isaiah 8:12-13; Genesis 6:1-4; Genesis 7:7; Genesis 7:13; 1 Enoch 21:10; 2 Peter 2:4-5; Jude 1:6; Ephesians 4:8-10; Ephesians 5:21-33; Colossians 3:18-19; Romans 6:3-4; Psalm 110:1; Matthew 5:10-12; Luke 6:28

settings.what: To wives, many with unbelieving husbands
settings.to: Christian wives in the churches, many married to men who did not share their faith, hearing the letter in the assembly
settings.when: The same letter, continuing the household code
settings.why: To guide women in a dangerous position, believers in households whose head had his own gods. They are to keep their faith, submit where they can, and let their lives speak. The passage speaks to Christian wives in Roman homes; how far 'submit' binds marriages today is debated (see the card at Ephesians 5).
views: Many read the call to submit as a lasting pattern for Christian marriage, grounded in Sarah's example.
Others read it as advice for wives of pagan husbands in a Roman setting, aimed at winning them, not as a rule for all marriages.

settings.why: To shape how husbands used their place at the head of the household: they must live with their wives with understanding, give them honor and treat them as equal heirs of grace, or their own prayers will be hindered.

settings.what: To all: blessing for abuse, and a ready defense
settings.when: While they were being slandered and threatened
settings.why: To shape how a slandered community responds: no revenge, blessing instead, no fear of opponents, and a gentle, reasoned answer for their hope. Psalm 34 gives the pattern of the righteous sufferer whom the Lord watches over.

settings.what: Christ's suffering, victory and the meaning of baptism (perhaps an early creed)
settings.by: Peter, perhaps using a creed or hymn
settings.to: The whole church, all of them baptized
settings.why: To ground the call to suffer for doing good in Christ's own path: he suffered unjustly, was made alive, proclaimed victory over the hostile spirits and now rules over every power. The readers, few like Noah's family, share that victory through their baptism. For people who felt powerless, the passage says the powers behind their persecutors are already under Christ.
views: Many scholars find in 3:18, 22 lines of an early confession: put to death, made alive, gone into heaven, at the right hand.
Others read the passage as Peter's own composition, written for this letter's theme of suffering and vindication.

traditions.q: What did Christ do when he 'went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison' (3:19)? (Where he 'came down' is the card at Ephesians 4:9.)
views: Christ 'descended there as Saviour, proclaiming the Good News to the spirits imprisoned there' (Catechism 632, citing 3:18-19). 'Jesus did not descend into hell to deliver the damned' but 'to free the just who had gone before him', 'these holy souls, who awaited their Saviour in Abraham's bosom' (633). The Catechism reads 4:6, 'the gospel was preached even to the dead', the same way (634). Thomas Aquinas set out this reading of 3:19 and then judged that Augustine 'furnishes a better exposition': the preaching 'is not to be referred to Christ's descent into hell' but to Christ's Godhead preaching to the unbelievers of Noah's day (Summa Theologiae III, question 52, article 2).

Hades is 'a spiritual prison', the state of spirits separated by sin from the sight of God's face. Christ descended into hell 'that he might there also preach his victory over death, and deliver the souls which with faith awaited his coming'; the catechism cites 3:18-19 as its proof (Philaret's Longer Catechism, questions 214-216).

The Formula of Concord notes that 'dissimilar explanations of the article concerning the descent of Christ to hell' are found among ancient teachers 'as well as in some among our teachers'. It teaches that 'the entire person, God and man' descended into hell 'after the burial', 'conquered the devil, destroyed the power of hell, and took from the devil all his might', and adds: 'We should not, however, trouble ourselves with high and acute thoughts as to how this occurred' (Solid Declaration, article 9). It does not cite 3:19.

Calvin's commentary takes the spirits as 'souls separated from their bodies' and says 'the manifestation of Christ's grace was made to godly spirits' who waited in hope. The Reformed catechisms explain the creed's clause in other ways. The Heidelberg Catechism (Q&A 44), whose proof texts do not include this verse, reads 'he descended to hell' of the 'unspeakable anguish, pain, and terror of soul' Christ suffered 'on the cross but also earlier', by which he 'has delivered me from hellish anguish and torment'. The Westminster Larger Catechism (Q. 50) reads it as Christ's 'continuing in the state of the dead, and under the power of death till the third day'.
Article 3 of the Thirty-Nine Articles: 'As Christ died for us, and was buried, so also is it to be believed, that he went down into Hell.' The article does not say what he did there.

Doctrine and Covenants 138 (a vision of Joseph F. Smith, 1918) quotes 3:18-20 and 4:6. It teaches that the Lord did not go in person among the wicked, but 'from among the righteous, he organized his forces and appointed messengers', and 'thus was the gospel preached to the dead', including those who died 'without a knowledge of the truth', who may receive 'vicarious baptism for the remission of sins'.

traditions.q: Baptism 'saves you now as well', yet 'not the removing of dirt from the flesh but the pledge of a good conscience made to God' (3:21). Does God save through the act of baptism, or is baptism the sign and pledge of a salvation received by faith? (On how the Greek of 3:21 can be parsed, see the note 'What saves'. Whether baptism is necessary for salvation is the card at Mark 16:16.)
views: 'The Church has seen in Noah's ark a prefiguring of salvation by Baptism', in which 'a few, that is, eight persons, were saved through water' (Catechism 1219). Baptism's 'two principal effects are purification from sins and new birth in the Holy Spirit' (1262): 'By Baptism all sins are forgiven, original sin and all personal sins, as well as all punishment for sin' (1263).

Philaret's Longer Catechism uses 3:20-21 for the Church: 'The Apostle Peter writes that baptism saveth us after the figure of the ark of Noah. All who were saved from the general deluge were saved only in the ark; so all who obtain everlasting salvation obtain it only in the one Catholic Church' (question 272). Baptism is a sacrament in which a believer, plunged three times in water in the name of the Trinity, 'dies to the carnal life of sin' and 'is born again of the Holy Ghost to a life spiritual and holy' (question 288).

Baptism 'works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe this'. 'It is not the water indeed that does them, but the word of God which is in and with the water, and faith, which trusts such word of God in the water' (Luther's Small Catechism).

'Does this outward washing with water itself wash away sins?' 'No, only Jesus Christ's blood and the Holy Spirit cleanse us from all sins' (Heidelberg Catechism, Q&A 72, citing this verse). Yet by 'this divine pledge and sign' God assures believers 'that we are as truly washed of our sins spiritually as our bodies are washed with water physically' (Q&A 73). Calvin, on this verse: 'the external symbol is not sufficient, except baptism be received really and effectually'.

Article 27 calls baptism 'a sign of Regeneration or new Birth, whereby, as by an instrument, they that receive Baptism rightly are grafted into the Church'. The 1662 Prayer Book's baptism prayer recalls that God 'didst save Noah and his family in the ark from perishing by water', 'figuring thereby thy holy Baptism', and after the baptism the priest says that the child 'is regenerate and grafted into the body of Christ's Church'.

'Christian baptism is the immersion of a believer in water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.' 'It is an act of obedience symbolizing the believer's faith in a crucified, buried, and risen Saviour', and it is 'prerequisite to the privileges of church membership and to the Lord's Supper' (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 7). Regeneration 'is a change of heart wrought by the Holy Spirit through conviction of sin, to which the sinner responds in repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus Christ', and 'There is no salvation apart from personal faith in Jesus Christ as Lord' (article 4). Neither article cites 3:21.

title: The Fiery Ordeal
sum: Since Christ suffered in the flesh, the readers are to arm themselves with the same intent and live the rest of their lives for God's will, not for the drinking and idol feasts of their past. Their old friends find it strange and slander them, but they will answer to the judge of the living and the dead; that is why the good news was announced even to the dead (4:1-6).

The end of all things is near: so pray, love one another without letting up, open your homes, and use every gift as good stewards, speaking God's words and serving in God's strength (4:7-11). The fiery ordeal is no strange thing: sharing Christ's sufferings is cause for joy, and to suffer 'as a Christian' is no shame. Judgment begins at God's house, so those who suffer should entrust themselves to the faithful Creator and keep doing good (4:12-19).
readings: Persecution under Rome

Read with Pliny's letter to Trajan from Bithynia-Pontus (around AD 112), 4:12-16 sounds like trials in which bearing the name 'Christian' was itself a charge. Scholars who date the letter late often read it this way.
Social hostility

Read with 4:3-4, the 'fiery ordeal' is the anger of former friends and families who felt rejected when converts stopped joining their feasts. This reading fits the letter's emphasis on slander and insults rather than courts and executions.
Suffering as the church's calling
Read theologically, the chapter makes suffering part of the Christian life itself: it unites believers with Christ, purifies the church as God's house, and is held within God's care as Creator.

views.H: The list in 4:3 describes city life: banquets, drinking parties and festivals in honor of the gods. Leaving them cut converts off from guilds, neighbors and family. Pliny, governor of Bithynia-Pontus about AD 112, asked Trajan whether 'the name itself' was to be punished, and Trajan replied that Christians 'are not to be sought out'.
views.C: 4:11 ends with a doxology and 'Amen', and 4:12 seems to start fresh, which raises the question whether the suffering of 4:12-19 is newer or fiercer than that of 1:6. The word 'Christian' (4:16) is used in dating the letter.
views.L: 'Suffered in the flesh' (4:1) picks up 3:18. 'Strange' links the neighbors who find the converts strange (4:4) with the converts who must not find the ordeal strange (4:12). The chapter has two endings that look toward God: a doxology (4:11) and the faithful Creator (4:19).
views.J: Judgment beginning at God's sanctuary is Ezekiel 9:6 and Jeremiah 25:29. Proverbs 10:12 and 11:31 are quoted, the second in its Greek form. The Spirit resting on the insulted (4:14) echoes Isaiah 11:2.
views.T: 4:6 has been read with 3:19 of Christ's descent to the dead. 4:10-11 has been used in teaching on spiritual gifts and ministry, and 4:8 on love and forgiveness.

deep.b: Three readings are common. (1) The same event as 3:19: Christ announced good news to the dead in the realm of the dead. The Catholic Catechism cites the verse this way (634), and Doctrine and Covenants 138 quotes it for the preaching of the gospel to the dead. (2) Christians who heard the good news while alive and have since died: people judged them, and they died like all humans, but God will give them life. Many modern commentators prefer this, because 4:5 speaks of the judgment of 'the living and the dead' and 4:6 explains why believers who died are not lost. (3) The spiritually dead, people dead in sin (compare Ephesians 2:1), an old reading that most modern scholars do not follow.

Peter's list is short: speaking and serving (4:11). Paul's lists are longer (Romans 12:6-8; 1 Corinthians 12). Both treat every believer as gifted and responsible for the others. The 'household managers' (4:10) are not a special class: 'each of you has been given a gift'. On speaking in tongues and the other gifts, see the topic Spiritual Gifts.

echoes: Proverbs 10:12; Proverbs 11:31; Isaiah 11:2; Ezekiel 9:6; Jeremiah 25:29; Malachi 3:1-5; Acts 10:42; Acts 11:26; Romans 12:6-13; James 5:20; Matthew 5:11-12; Luke 23:46; Psalm 31:5; Romans 13:12-13

settings.to: Converts, probably most of them Gentiles, whose former friends mocked them for leaving the feasts
settings.why: To give converts a way to see the mockery: they share Christ's suffering, they have broken with their old life on purpose, and those who slander them will answer to God.

settings.what: The end is near: prayer, love, hospitality, gifts
settings.when: In the expectation that 'the end of all things has come close'
settings.why: To turn expectation of the end into community life: clear-headed prayer, love that covers sins, homes open to travelers, and every gift used for others. A pressured minority survives by caring for its own.

settings.what: The fiery ordeal and the name 'Christian'
settings.to: The same churches, now addressed as facing a fiery test
settings.when: A time of insults and perhaps accusations 'as a Christian'
settings.why: To keep believers from being shaken or ashamed: suffering for the name is a share in Christ's suffering and a sign that the Spirit rests on them. It also warns them not to give real cause for punishment.
views: Some read 4:12 as news that a new, fiercer persecution had begun.
Others read it as a renewed look at the trials already described (1:6), now pictured as fire.

title: The Chief Shepherd and the Roaring Lion
sum: Peter, a fellow elder and witness of Christ's sufferings, urges the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for money and not as lords, but as examples, awaiting the Chief Shepherd's unfading wreath of glory (5:1-4). The younger are to submit to the elders, and all are to tie on humility, because God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble (5:5).

They are to humble themselves under God's strong hand, throw their worries on him, stay alert, and stand against the devil, who prowls like a roaring lion, knowing that believers everywhere suffer the same (5:6-9). The God of all grace will restore and strengthen them (5:10-11). The letter ends with Silvanus, greetings from 'her who is in Babylon' and from Mark, and the kiss of love (5:12-14).
readings: A letter from Rome
Read with early Christian tradition, 'Babylon' is Rome, Peter is there with Mark and Silvanus, and the letter is a word from the church at the empire's center to churches in the provinces.
Leadership as service

Read as instructions for church leaders, 5:1-5 gives one of the New Testament's clearest pictures of pastoral work: shepherding, overseeing, not domineering, setting an example, all under the Chief Shepherd.
The last battle
Read with Job and Revelation, the devil as accuser and roaring lion stands behind the readers' slanderers, and the God of all grace promises the end of their suffering.

views.H: Elders led house churches; 'shameful gain' suggests they handled money. Mark and Silvanus are known from Acts and Paul's letters. Eusebius reports that Papias and Clement of Alexandria said Peter wrote this letter in Rome and called the city Babylon.
views.C: 5:12 ('through Silvanus') is central to the authorship debate: Silvanus as secretary, as courier, or as part of a pseudonymous frame. 'Babylon' as a name for Rome is found in Revelation; Bart Ehrman and others hold that the name came into use only after Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, and use it to date the letter later.
views.L: The shepherd image closes a thread begun in 2:25 ('the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls'). The letter ends where it began: chosen (1:1; 5:13), grace (1:2; 5:12), peace (1:2; 5:14), and exile (the Dispersion and Babylon).
views.J: God's strong hand (Deuteronomy 7:8; 26:8), Proverbs 3:34, Psalm 55:22 and the accuser of Job and Zechariah are all from Israel's Scriptures. 'Babylon' recalls the exile. The elders echo Israel's elders and the synagogue's leaders.
views.T: 5:1-4 is read in Catholic and Orthodox tradition with Peter's place among the apostles; Protestants stress 'fellow elder'. 5:13 is the main New Testament text for Peter's presence in Rome.

deep.b: The New Testament never says that Peter went to Rome, except through 5:13 if 'Babylon' means Rome. The earliest outside evidence is from Rome itself: 1 Clement (about AD 96) says that Peter 'endured not one or two, but numerous labours' and 'suffered martyrdom' (chapter 5), and Ignatius of Antioch (about AD 110) wrote to the Romans, 'I do not, as Peter and Paul, issue commandments unto you' (To the Romans 4). Eusebius (about AD 325) reports from Clement of Alexandria and Papias that Peter wrote this letter 'in Rome itself' and called the city 'by a figure, Babylon', and elsewhere that Peter was 'crucified head-downwards' in Rome (Church History 2.15; 3.1). Ancient tradition from 1 Clement on thus places Peter's death in Rome; what that means for the papacy is a separate question (see the card at Matthew 16:18).

Silvanus is very likely Silas, a leader of the Jerusalem church sent with the apostles' letter to Antioch (Acts 15:22), who then traveled with Paul (Acts 15:40) and is named in 1 Thessalonians 1:1. Mark is very likely the John Mark of Acts 12:12, whose mother's house was a meeting place of the Jerusalem church, and who later worked with Paul (Philemon 1:24; 2 Timothy 4:11). If both were with Peter in Rome, the letter joins the Jerusalem church, Paul's mission and Peter. Eusebius preserves the tradition from Papias that Mark wrote down Peter's preaching; see the topic Gospel of Mark.

echoes: John 21:15-17; Acts 20:28; Mark 10:42-45; Proverbs 3:34; James 4:6-10; Psalm 55:22; Matthew 6:25-34; Job 1:7; Zechariah 3:1; Psalm 22:13; Revelation 14:8; Revelation 17:5; Acts 12:12; Acts 15:22; Romans 16:16

settings.to: The elders who led the house churches of the five regions
settings.when: The same letter, in a time of suffering
settings.why: To make sure leaders under pressure did not become either hirelings or tyrants: they were to shepherd God's flock willingly, honestly and by example, accountable to Christ the Chief Shepherd. The call binds church leaders; how 'elder' relates to 'overseer' and later offices is debated (see the topic Elders).
views: Catholic and Orthodox readers see Peter's exhortation to the elders of five regions as an exercise of his apostolic office.
Many Protestant readers stress that Peter calls himself only a fellow elder and gives a model of plural, servant leadership.

settings.what: To the younger, and to all: humility and vigilance
settings.to: The younger members first, then the whole church
settings.why: To hold the community together under pressure: the young respecting leaders, all serving each other in humility, all trusting God with their worries and standing against the devil, the true enemy behind their slanderers.

settings.to: The churches of the five regions
settings.when: At the end of the letter, from 'Babylon'
settings.why: To name the letter's bearer or writer, to sum up its purpose ('this is God's true grace. Stand in it') and to join the readers to the church in 'Babylon' and to Mark, so that scattered believers know they belong to one family across the empire.
views: The common view, reported by Eusebius from Papias and Clement of Alexandria.
Erasmus and Calvin took it as the city in Mesopotamia.
